questions.question: List the specifications of the Starship vehicle. Five facts needed: total height, total liftoff mass, total liftoff thrust, number of first-stage engines, number of upper-stage engines.
Why is the chopstick-catch approach more ambitious than leg-landing, and what engineering capabilities had to be proven before attempting the catch?
expected_reasoning_chain: Falcon 9 uses landing legs, which adds mass and structure to the rocket
Legs require a wider landing zone and a slower terminal velocity, which the booster can achieve with its 1 Merlin vacuum engine
Super Heavy has 33 Raptor engines, of which only the 13 center engines can be used for the catch burn (the outer 20 are not gimbaling-correct for landing)
The catch requires the booster to slide into the tower's mechanical arms at near-zero vertical velocity, which means a much more precise hover-and-slide maneuver than leg landing
The booster must arrive at the catch point with a positional accuracy of ~30 cm
Before attempting the catch, SpaceX had to prove the 13-engine hover-and-slide could work, which required multiple IFTs (3, 4) to demonstrate reliable booster return
Therefore the catch was a 3-flight iteration: demonstrate return (IFT-3, 4), then attempt catch (IFT-5) — not a first-flight aspiration
questions.scoring_hint: credit 0.15 per chain element mentioned; 1.0 for 6+ elements

questions.question: Why did IFT-6 catch the booster successfully but lose the ship during the same mission, and what does the pattern of ship failures tell us about the engineering maturity of the two stages?
expected_reasoning_chain: IFT-6 successfully caught the Super Heavy booster for the second time
The Starship upper stage lost contact before its planned splashdown
SpaceX attributed the loss to a propellant leak that developed during the coast phase
The booster has been retrieved successfully 3 times (IFT-5, 6, 7), suggesting the Super Heavy stage is at a higher engineering maturity
The ship has been retrieved only once (IFT-7); in 4 of 5 flights the ship was lost
The pattern suggests: the booster is more mature because the catch mechanics have been iterated on since IFT-5
The ship is less mature because it has more complex re-entry and landing requirements (more systems, more failure modes)
Therefore IFT-6 is a normal iterative development outcome: one stage (booster) is now production-quality, the other (ship) is still being refined
questions.scoring_hint: credit 0.12 per chain element; 1.0 for 7+ elements

questions.question: Summarize the SpaceX Starship 2024–2025 test campaign in exactly 5 bullet points, covering: the vehicle, the early test flights, the catch breakthrough, the January 2025 milestone, and the broader industry impact.
expected_topics: Vehicle: 121m tall Starship with 33-engine Super Heavy booster, full reuse design with chopstick-catch on launch tower, total liftoff mass ~5000t, thrust ~7500t — most powerful rocket ever built

Early test flights: IFT-3 (March 2024) reached space at 234 km but lost on re-entry; IFT-4 (June 2024) achieved first controlled re-entry with 1500°C peak heating survived; IFT-5 (October 2024) first booster catch at Starbase
Catch breakthrough: chopstick arms on the launch tower caught the 200t Super Heavy booster at near-zero vertical velocity, a 30cm positional accuracy maneuver, no precedent in spaceflight

January 2025 milestone (IFT-7): first time both stages of an orbital launch system were caught on the same launch tower — the ship was caught by a second tower after a 37-minute coast, proving rapid full reuse is feasible

Broader impact: every other launch provider (SLS, Vulcan, New Glenn, Neutron, Ariane 6) is now revising architecture to compete with or partner on full reuse; the test campaign is the textbook example of SpaceX's iterative design philosophy
questions.scoring_hint: human review: credit 0.2 per topic covered; 1.0 for all 5
